comparator.name: Maastricht Science Programme (BSc)
comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027 (Education and Examination Regulations of the Maastricht School of Liberal Arts and Sciences 2026-2027, MSP programme, Articles 3.6-3.10 and Appendix I; MSP Course Catalogue 2025-2026, the latest published; programme pages checked 2026-10-05)
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme pages (s2, s3, s4) describe the English-taught, three-year, full-time bachelor in words and give no EC. The 180-EC reconstruction therefore uses the 2026-2027 Education and Examination Regulations of the Maastricht School of Liberal Arts and Sciences (s0), which cover the MSP programme: Article 3.6 (180 EC), 3.7 (components), 3.8 (core of four 5-EC courses plus core skills trainings and projects of 10 EC, and a general education of two 5-EC courses, one in mathematics and one humanities or social-science topic), 3.10 (elective curriculum of fourteen 5-EC courses, eight 2.5-EC skills trainings and four 5-EC projects, and a 30-EC Bachelor Thesis Research in the final semester) and Appendix I (core courses BIO1101, CHE1101, PHY1101 and INT1101, core skills trainings PRA1101 and PRA1102 of 2.5 EC each and core project PRO1101). The MSP Course Catalogue 2025-2026 (s1), the latest catalogue published and the one the curriculum page links to, confirms 5 EC per course and project and 2.5 EC per skills training. Totals: core 20 + 5 + 5 = 30 EC, general education 10 EC, elective courses 70 EC, skills 20 EC, projects 20 EC and thesis 30 EC, which is 180 EC with 20 courses, 10 skills trainings, five projects and the thesis. The programme has no formal routes, tracks or concentrations: after the core each student builds a personal profile, so no route is selected. The elective curriculum, a mathematics choice and a humanities or social-science choice are genuinely open and are preserved as restricted-choice components with their actual EC rather than filled with invented courses. The Regulations do not place components in particular years; the curriculum page describes each semester as two seven-week periods followed by a three-week project period, and the thesis is fixed to the final semester. The catalogue text for the core courses could not be read reliably from the PDF layout, so core components other than PRA1101 and PRA1102 are characterised by title and the Regulations only. No 2026-2027 catalogue was found, so the 2025-2026 catalogue is the most recent course evidence.

alternatives.concept: The Maastricht Science Programme has no fixed curriculum beyond its core: every student completes introductory courses in biology, chemistry, physics and liberal arts and sciences, a mathematics course and a humanities or social-science course, then builds a personal science profile from fourteen elective courses, eight skills trainings and four projects, with at least four 3000-level courses, before a 30-EC Bachelor Thesis Research. The generic programme has no formal route. This alternative reproduces the part of that structure that UCR's catalogue can support: biology and biochemistry foundations with laboratory training; ecology, evolution and Earth-system science applied to energy, health and sustainability challenges; mathematics, statistics, numerical and systems methods with programming and data analysis; experimental design and a team research project; and 300-level work in pathology, genetics, biogeochemistry, statistics and linear systems. UCR has no chemistry, physics or materials course, so those parts of the core and of the profile cannot be reproduced; biochemistry and biogeochemistry are the nearest chemistry content and Earth-system and linear-systems courses the nearest physical-science content.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum has six life-science courses (Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine; Molecular Cell Biology; Human Physiology; Biochemistry; Life Science Laboratory; Molecular Pathology & Genetics), nine ecology, earth-system and sustainability courses (Sustainability Essentials I, The Science of Evolution, Ecosystems Uncovered, Sustainable Farming & Innovation, Dynamic Earth, Earth System Science Tools, Environmental Biogeochemistry, Climate Change, Research in a Sustainable Delta), seven mathematics, statistics, programming and data courses (Introduction to Programming, Mathematical Methods, Linear Algebra, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems, Probability & Statistics, Introduction to Data Science), Research Methods & Statistics and Personal & Professional Development. No single field dominates and UCR has no chemistry, physics or materials course, so the label names the life-science, earth and environmental science and the mathematics and data analysis together and does not present the programme as a natural-science degree with chemistry and physics.

alternatives.concept: The programme lists neurosciences as a formal study direction that students can build a science profile around, alongside biology, chemistry, physics and mathematics and interdisciplinary fields such as biomedical engineering. This alternative takes that direction as its organising logic: a neuroscience and cognitive-neuroscience sequence from the gateway course through neurobiology, perception and action, higher-order functions and the neuroscience of language, supported by human biology, cell biology, biochemistry, physiology, anatomy and disease mechanisms, pharmacology and immunity, with statistics, experimental research methods, systematic review, mathematics and data analysis as the research training. It preserves the programme's laboratory and research emphasis through the Life Science Laboratory and the research-methods courses, and it cannot reproduce the chemistry and physics of the core or the MSP's computational neuroscience and neural-circuit courses.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum has five neuroscience and cognition courses (Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Neurobiology, Perception & Action, Higher Order Functions, Psycholinguistics), six biomedical and human-biology courses (Functional Anatomy, Pharmacology, Infection & Immunity, Mechanisms of Disease, Human Physiology, Molecular Pathology & Genetics), four life-science foundation courses (Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine; Molecular Cell Biology; Biochemistry; Life Science Laboratory), two research-methods courses (Statistics & Experimental Methods, Advanced Research Seminar), six mathematics and data courses (Mathematical Methods, Linear Algebra, Linear Systems, Probability & Statistics, Introduction to Data Science, Neural Networks & Deep Learning) and Personal & Professional Development. Neuroscience and biomedical science together dominate, so the label names both and the mathematics and statistics; it does not claim a full neuroscience degree because UCR has no computational-neuroscience or neural-circuit course.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Alternative 1 is organised around the programme's interdisciplinary core and an ecology, earth-system and sustainability profile with mathematics and data analysis, and contains no neuroscience or cognition course. Alternative 2 is organised around the neurosciences direction (row 6438): it drops all nine of Alternative 1's ecology, earth-system and sustainability courses and its project course, and instead adds Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Neurobiology, Perception & Action, Higher Order Functions, Psycholinguistics, Functional Anatomy, Pharmacology, Infection & Immunity, Mechanisms of Disease, Statistics & Experimental Methods, Advanced Research Seminar and Neural Networks & Deep Learning. It shares 12 courses with Alternative 1 (the life-science foundations and the mathematics and data core), so 12 courses (90 EC) are unique to it and 12 courses (90 EC) are unique to Alternative 1, well above the 30 EC / 4-course floor.

alternatives.concept: The programme names biomedical engineering and systems biology as interdisciplinary profiles, and describes imaging, signals and modelling among its courses and its graduates' master's directions. This alternative takes that direction as its organising logic: life-science and physiological foundations (cell biology, biochemistry, physiology, anatomy, disease mechanisms, genetics, neurobiology) combined with a quantitative core of programming, calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, linear systems and probability and statistics, and with data-science, machine-learning, image-processing, algorithm and optimisation methods applied to biological and biomedical data. It preserves the laboratory element through the Life Science Laboratory, and UCR has no biomedical-engineering, biomaterials, systems-biology or bioinformatics course, so the computational and quantitative courses implement the modelling and imaging side of the direction rather than substitute for those courses.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Alternative 1 is an ecology, earth-system and sustainability profile and Alternative 2 a neuroscience and biomedical profile; neither contains machine learning, image processing, advanced calculus, numerical methods beyond Alternative 1's single course, algorithms or optimisation. Alternative 3 is organised around the biomedical-engineering and systems-biology directions (rows 6439 and 6441): it replaces Alternative 1's nine ecology, earth-system and sustainability courses and Alternative 2's neuroscience sequence with Machine Learning, Image Processing & Computer Vision, Advanced Calculus, Algorithms & Data Structures and Optimization Methods in AI plus the modelling mathematics. It shares 14 courses with Alternative 1 and 17 with Alternative 2, so at least 7 courses (52.5 EC) are unique to it and unique to each of the others, above the 30 EC / 4-course floor.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Every formal prerequisite is scheduled in an earlier semester: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine and Sustainability Essentials I (semester 1) precede Molecular Cell Biology, Human Physiology, Biochemistry, Molecular Pathology & Genetics, Environmental Biogeochemistry and Earth System Science Tools, and Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Linear Algebra, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems and Probability & Statistics. Advisory progression is respected: introductory biology, programming, earth science and mathematics come first, cell biology and research methods follow in semester 2, the 300-level pathology, biogeochemistry, linear-systems and project courses come in semesters 4 and 5, and the laboratory course comes at the end after its biochemical background. Personal & Professional Development is in Year 1.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Every formal prerequisite is scheduled in an earlier semester: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine and Introduction to Programming (semester 1) precede Molecular Cell Biology, Functional Anatomy, Human Physiology and the other courses that require them, Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Linear Algebra, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems, Advanced Calculus, Probability & Statistics and Neural Networks & Deep Learning, and Introduction to Programming precedes Optimization Methods in AI. Advanced calculus, neural networks and optimisation are placed in semester 6 after the mathematics and programming foundation. Advisory progression is respected: Introduction to Data Science (semester 1) precedes Machine Learning and Image Processing, and cell biology and physiology precede the 300-level genetics and disease courses. Biochemistry is in semester 5 because its odd-semester offerings in semesters 1 and 3 were already full. Personal & Professional Development is in Year 1.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Three UCR alternatives are defensible and the maximum was reached. The Maastricht Science Programme has no formal route, so the closest response (Alternative 1) reproduces its structure as far as UCR allows: biology and biochemistry foundations, ecology and Earth-system science applied to energy, health and sustainability, mathematics, statistics and data analysis, laboratory and research-project training and advanced work. It owns seven generator-eligible rows: 6430 (interdisciplinary natural science), 6431 (scientific challenges in energy, health and sustainability), 6432 (independent scientific research), 6433 (laboratory experiments), 6434 (biology), 6437 (mathematics) and 6445 (designing original research projects). Alternative 2 is built on the neurosciences direction (6438) and Alternative 3 on the biomedical-engineering and systems-biology directions (6439 and 6441); they share 12 and 14 courses with Alternative 1 and 17 with each other, and each differs from every other alternative by at least 7 courses (52.5 EC), so every pair passes the 30 EC / 4-course floor. The fourth direction, chemistry, physics, biobased materials and nanomaterials (rows 6435, 6436, 6440 and 6442), was rejected as not-feasible: UCR has no chemistry, physics or materials-science course (its nearest content, Biochemistry and Environmental Biogeochemistry, is already in Alternative 1), so any alternative would relabel biology and earth-science courses as chemistry or physics. The support-only rows 6443 and 6444 strengthen the research and data-analysis courses; the search-only rows 6446 to 6468 (past thesis topics and graduate destinations) generated no alternative; no row is inherited across split targets.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both give the foundational biology of living systems; Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine covers the building blocks of life and how cells, molecules and systems interact, which is the primary subject of Introduction to Biology, whereas the Maastricht core course is taught alongside chemistry and physics in the three-field core.

Both address chemistry; Biochemistry teaches the chemistry of life, its reactions and the molecules of proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids, which is an important and identifiable part of Introduction to Chemistry, but UCR offers no general, organic or physical chemistry and the Maastricht course is introductory chemistry in general.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no physics course; the closest physical-science content (Dynamic Earth, Linear Systems) does not address the primary subject of Introduction to Physics.

Both train experimental laboratory skills; Life Science Laboratory teaches biochemical and molecular laboratory work with laboratory methods, experimental procedures and data analysis, which is an important part of the integrated biology and chemistry experiment in Introduction to Scientific Research I, although its themes are biomedical rather than chemical.

Both teach experimental design and the analysis of data; Research Methods & Statistics covers research logic, experimental design, laboratory research techniques and statistics, which is an important part of Introduction to Scientific Research II, but the Maastricht skills training is practical laboratory work.

Both are small-team research projects in which students design and carry out a study and report it; Research in a Sustainable Delta is a 300-level partner-based sustainability project whereas Introduction to Project Period is a three-week introductory project.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Introduction to Liberal Arts and Sciences is the programme's own introduction to the liberal arts and sciences approach to natural science and no UCR course serves that function; Personal & Professional Development is mandatory first-year study skills and is not matched to it.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the mathematics general education is a restricted choice of any MAT course that the sources do not name; the UCR mathematics courses appear in their own block without being forced onto this open component.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the humanities or social-science topic is a restricted choice from named MSP courses that have no UCR counterpart in this programme.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the fourteen elective courses are the student's own profile choice and the sources name no courses; the UCR course blocks above show the profile each UCR alternative builds without forcing it onto this open space.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the eight elective skills trainings are open choices that the sources do not name; UCR has no skills-training format.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the four elective project periods are open three-week projects; UCR has no project-period format and Research in a Sustainable Delta is matched to the core project.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the 30-EC Bachelor Thesis Research is an individual research project concluding the programme; UCR has no scheduled thesis course, and the standardized optional independent research element is shown against this component.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial study of biology, mathematics, statistics and data analysis and train students in experimental research. The Maastricht Science Programme additionally includes introductory chemistry and physics in its core and lets students build elective profiles in chemistry, physics, biobased materials, nanomaterials and neurosciences with laboratory skills trainings, project periods and a 30-EC Bachelor Thesis Research. UCR students can instead combine life-science, earth and environmental science, neuroscience, mathematics and data-science courses, but UCR offers no chemistry, physics or materials course and no thesis course at the same level of depth.

The Maastricht Science Programme organizes study around a fixed natural-science core followed by a largely open elective curriculum of courses, skills trainings and three-week projects and a one-semester thesis. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across courses in life science, ecology and earth science, neuroscience, mathematics and data science. The UCR programmes therefore cover related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the Maastricht programme course by course, and each UCR alternative stands for one possible elective profile.
